a system-on-chip is a general-purpose computer serving multiple purposes

A micro-
controller is usually simpler and more limited in hardware resources as
it specializes only in one purpose when running, whereas a system-
on-chip is a general-purpose computer that can serve multiple purposes.

query: Why does XFS keep two B+trees for free space in each allocation group, and why is the duplication not usually a problem?
expected_answer: One B+tree sorts free space by starting block number and the other by length, so the file system can find space by proximity to allocated space or by size needed. The duplication could cause inconsistencies if the trees get out of sync, but because XFS is journaled this is not generally an issue.
expected_facts: one B+tree sorted by starting block number
the other sorted by length
allows finding space by proximity or by size
duplication can cause inconsistency if trees get out of sync
journaling means this is not generally an issue

relevant_passages.quote: One of the B+trees records free space sorted by starting block number. The other B+tree sorts the free blocks by their length.
This duplication can cause inconsistencies if, for whatever reason, the two trees get out of sync. Because XFS is journaled, however, this is not generally an issue.

query: what happens in NTFS when the log fills up?
expected_answer: The log file service returns a "log file full" error to NTFS, which raises an exception, reschedules the operation, and asks the cache manager to flush unwritten data to disk. This lets uncompleted transactions finish and frees up log space.
expected_facts: log file service returns a "log file full" error to NTFS
NTFS raises an exception and reschedules the operation
cache manager is asked to flush unwritten data
flushing lets transactions complete and frees log space

if the log becomes full, the log ﬁle service will return
a “log ﬁle full” error to NTFS. NTFS then raises an exception, reschedules
the operation, and asks the cache manager to ﬂush unwritten data to disk.

query: Why did the disk fragmenter delete every other file it created?
expected_answer: When it got an out-of-disk space error, the disk fragmenter went back and deleted every other file it created, which on BFS perfectly fragmented the disk. By matching file size to the block size, it could leave every other disk block allocated, testing the block allocation policies.
expected_facts: triggered on out-of-disk space error
deletes every other file created
perfectly fragments the disk on BFS
tests block allocation policies

relevant_passages.quote:
The disk fragmenter would create ﬁles of either random or ﬁxed size, some
number per directory, and when it received an out-of-disk space error it would
go back and delete every other ﬁle it created.

In the case of BFS this perfectly
fragmented a disk, and by adjusting the size of the created ﬁles to match the
ﬁle system block size, it was possible to leave the disk with every other disk
block allocated.

query: Why does Oberon avoid overlapping windows in favour of tiled viewers?
expected_answer: Partially hidden windows are typically brought to the top before any operation is applied, so the advantage is insignificant compared with the substantial implementation effort; tiled viewers are much simpler and have no genuine disadvantages.
expected_facts: overlapping windows offer insignificant advantage
substantial effort to implement
tiled viewers are simpler with no genuine disadvantages

relevant_passages.quote: Partially hidden windows are typically brought to the top and made fully visible before any operation is applied to their contents.
Therefore, we have chosen a solution that is much simpler to realize, yet has no genuine disadvantages compared to overlapping windows: tiled viewers as shown in Fig. 2.1.

query: How can Oberon be a single-process system and still let a user work on several tasks at once, and where do task switches happen?
expected_answer: Tasks appear as viewers, and the user switches between them implicitly by choosing a different viewer as operand for the next command. Task switches therefore occur only between commands, at user-defined points, while the processor polls event sources in a central loop.
expected_facts: tasks are manifest as viewers
user switches by choosing a different viewer as operand
task switches occur between commands only
central loop polls event sources

relevant_passages.quote: The user switches between tasks implicitly when choosing a different viewer as operand for the next command.

The essential difference between Oberon and multiprocess-systems is that in the former task switches occur between commands only, whereas in the latter a switch may be invoked after any single instruction.

locks are dispensable and deadlocks are not a topic

Locks of common resources are co mpletely dispensable and deadlocks are not a topic.

query: Why does the first barrier attempt deadlock when n = 5 and 4 threads are already waiting?
expected_answer: When the 5th thread signals the barrier, only one waiting thread is allowed to proceed and the semaphore goes from -4 to -3. No one signals again, so the other threads can never pass the barrier.

no one signals again, so the others stay blocked (deadlock)

But then no one signals the semaphore again and none of the oth er threads can pass the barrier.

query: What is a turnstile and what state does it start in?

can be locked to bar all threads

relevant_passages.quote: This pattern, a wait and a signal in rapid succession, occurs often enough that it has a name; it’s called a turnstile, because it allows one thread to pass at a time, and it can be locked to bar all threads.

This is not just a question of injustice; it is possible for mo re than 5 threads to be in the critical section concurrently, which violates t he synchronization constraints.
